title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges per user, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to retain full ownership of their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively simple to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large enterprises, while Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration: Jira has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited set of integrations, including GitHub and GitLab.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Robust project management features
* Scalable for large enterprises
* User-friendly interface
* Extensive customer support
### Plane
* Free and self-hosted
* Full data ownership and control
* Simple setup process
* Customizable workflows
* Open-source community support
However, Plane has limited integrations and a smaller user community compared to Jira.

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large enterprises with complex project management needs and a large budget. It offers a wide range of integrations and a robust set of features that can handle large-scale projects. On the other hand, Plane is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that want more control over their data and are looking for a cost-effective solution. It is ideal for teams with simple project management needs and a limited budget.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane instance on your server.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Configure your workflows and customize your Plane instance as needed.
5. Test your Plane instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and integrations that Jira offers. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane has limited support for agile project management methodologies. However, for teams that value data ownership and are looking for a cost-effective solution, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced project management features
* Teams with limited budgets that want to reduce costs
* Teams that value data ownership and control
* Teams with simple project management needs
* Teams that do not require integrations with third-party tools

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Jira?
No, Jira is not available for self-hosting.
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and open-source.
### Can I import my Jira data into Plane?
Yes, you can import your Jira data into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Does Plane have a user-friendly interface?
Yes, Plane has a simple and user-friendly interface.
### Is Plane suitable for large enterprises?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large enterprises due to its limited features and integrations.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Asana vs Taiga
comparison_markdown:
# Asana vs Taiga (2026)

## Overview
Asana and Taiga are project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Asana who are considering switching to Taiga, possibly due to the desire for more control over their data or the need for a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration and task management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their project management platform.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Asana offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10.99 per user, while Taiga is free and open-source, with the option for self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Taiga allows for full data ownership and control, while Asana stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Asana is generally easier to set up and use, with a more user-friendly interface, while Taiga requires more technical expertise, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both tools can handle large teams and projects, but Taiga's self-hosting option provides more flexibility for scaling.
* Integration difference: Asana has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party tools, while Taiga has a more limited but still growing list of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Asana | Taiga |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10.99+/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $10.99 * 50 = $549.50 | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $10.99 * 200 = $2198 | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Asana
* Easy to use and set up
* Extensive library of integrations
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
### Taiga
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Highly customizable
* Active community of developers
* Limited integrations with third-party tools
* Requires technical expertise for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
Asana is a good choice for teams who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party tools. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, from small startups to large enterprises, and is particularly well-suited for teams who don't require full control over their data. Taiga, on the other hand, is ideal for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and customizing their project management platform. It's particularly well-suited for teams who require a high degree of customization and flexibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Asana in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Taiga instance, either on a self-hosted server or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the Taiga import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure your Taiga instance to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly and that your team can use the new platform effectively.

## Our Take
Taiga is a production-ready platform for teams who value data ownership and control, but it may not be the best choice for teams who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Taiga's self-hosting option requires a significant amount of technical expertise, which can be a barrier for teams without dedicated IT resources. We recommend switching to Taiga if you're a team of 10-50 users who values data ownership and control, and is willing to invest time and resources into setting up and customizing your project management platform.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who value data ownership and control
* Teams with dedicated IT resources who can handle self-hosting and customization
* Teams who don't require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Teams who prioritize customization and flexibility in their project management platform
* Teams who are currently using Asana's free plan and want to avoid paying per-user fees

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Taiga on my own server?
Yes, Taiga can be self-hosted on your own server, giving you full control over your data and platform.
### Is Taiga free?
Yes, Taiga is free and open-source, with no per-user fees or costs.

Yes, Taiga provides an import tool that allows you to import your data from Asana in CSV or JSON format.

Not yet, but the Taiga team is working on developing a mobile app for iOS and Android devices.
